newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai Airways seen soaring after baht float.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai Airways seen soaring after baht float.

text.p: Thai Airways International, (THAI) whose income is about 75 percent dollar-based, is seen flying higher after the baht's de facto devaluation, analysts said on Friday.
They expect the national flag carrier, which posted disappointing first-half results, to show an improvement from the second half of this year as a result of the baht's managed float.

ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett Asia forecast that THAI's net profit in 1998 fiscal year (October-September) would nearly double to 5.95 billion baht ($205.2 million) from a projected 2.87 billion baht this year.
Thailand last week scrapped the baht's peg against a trade-weighted basket of currencies and allowed the currency to move under a new managed float system.
The move, which saw the baht plummet 15-20 percent, has forced many other Thai corporates with foreign debt exposure into vulnerable loss-making positions.
But they said THAI was one of the few exceptions. The company's revenue and cost structure puts it in a unique position to increase net free cash flow after the baht float.
The company's business is largely protected from the domestic economic chaos which usually follows a currency devaluation.
"Interestingly, THAI's business is relatively impervious to domestic economic chaos that a baht devaluation would create," said a report from Paribas Asia Equity.

As the Asian representative of Star Alliance, a consortium of airlines whose route network is the world's largest, the airline has an international customer base which would be unaffected by baht devaluation.
Star Alliance is a new partnership between THAI, United Airlines, Lufthansa, Scandinavian Airlines System and Ansett of Australia.

Although the de facto devaluation means the company's foreign debt, around 65 percent of which is in U.S. dollars will rise, the airline has a specific accounting policy for dealing with gains or losses in the translation of foreign currency loans.
As a state enterprise, the airline will not write off the entire foreign exchange loss on its foreign borrowing through its profit and loss account.

"Instead, the company will adjust its debt and increase its deferred forex reserve by the entire loss. The loss will be gradually amortised ... over the life of each of the company's loans," said Paribas Asia Equity's report.
At the end of September 1996, the airline had net borrowings of 74.2 billion baht. It posted net profits of 3.38 billion baht in the year ended September 30, 1996 versus 3.24 billion a year earlier.
THAI was actively traded on Friday after surging earlier this week on its prospects. Its share price closed down five baht at 55.00, well up on its June 30 close of 38 baht.
